meta.title: Who really said "I have ways of making money that you know nothing of"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Disputed. It reaches us through one witness at an 1879 hearing; Rockefeller doubted he ever said it, and the line closely echoes John 4:32.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have ways of making money that you know nothing of'?
meta.ogDescription: A single witness, an 1879 hearing, and a denial. Wikiquote files this Rockefeller line under Disputed — and it echoes a famous verse from John.

answer.label: Disputed — one witness’s recollection, which Rockefeller denied
answer.sourceLine: This is not a quotation from anything Rockefeller wrote or published. It reaches us as reported speech: Wikiquote ↗ files it under Disputed, recording it as quoted by Isaac Hewitt in 1879 testimony to the New York Assembly, and notes that Rockefeller doubted he had said it — citing David Freeman Hawke’s John D.: The Founding Father of the Rockefellers (1980). Wikiquote also flags that the line echoes John 4:32 ↗.

source.heading: What the attribution actually rests on

docMeta.dd: Testimony of Isaac Hewitt, New York Assembly, 1879

source.excerpt: I have ways of making money that you know nothing of.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ does not treat this as a genuine Rockefeller quotation. It sits in the Disputed section, with the attribution given as Isaac Hewitt’s 1879 testimony to the New York Assembly and an explicit note that Rockefeller doubted saying it, sourced to David Freeman Hawke, John D.: The Founding Father of the Rockefellers (1980). The single genuinely supporting witness is therefore a recollection recorded decades after the events it describes.

We tried to reach the testimony itself and could not. The 1879 New York investigation is the Hepburn committee, whose proceedings are digitized; we searched six volumes of them and found no Isaac Hewitt at all — the only Hewitt in the text is Abraham S. Hewitt, a different man — and no sentence resembling this one the proceedings on archive.org ↗. That is not proof of absence: these are OCR scans, we did not search every volume, and the testimony may sit in a different record. But we could not confirm the citation, and we are not going to assert a locator we did not read.

The name is at least plausible. Rockefeller’s first job, in September 1855, was as an assistant bookkeeper at a small Cleveland produce commission firm called Hewitt & Tuttle Wikipedia on his early career ↗. Whether the Isaac Hewitt of the testimony is that Hewitt is an inference we cannot source, and we leave it as one.
source.excerptNote: Set this beside the King James rendering of John 4:32 — “But he said unto them, I have meat to eat that ye know not of.” The shape is the same, and Wikiquote itself raises the parallel. That does not prove the remark was invented, but it does mean the sentence had a ready-made template in the most widely read book in nineteenth-century America.

source.rightsNote: We are asserting no rights status here, because we could not establish where the words were first published. If the 1879 testimony citation is correct, the underlying text would be a New York State legislative record from 1879 and free of copyright — but we were unable to locate it, and Hawke’s 1980 biography, which is the source actually in hand for the denial, is a modern in-copyright work. This is not legal advice.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.heading: About John D. Rockefeller
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller Sr. (1839–1937) founded Standard Oil in 1870 and built it into the dominant force in American oil, before spending his later decades giving the money away through foundations, universities and medical research institutes. He was also, for thirty years, one of the most investigated men in the country — which matters here, because a great deal of what he is quoted as saying survives only as other people’s testimony about him, given under oath and often by opponents.

misattribution.heading: Why this one is doubted
misattribution.intro: Nothing here is fabricated outright — but every leg the attribution stands on is weaker than the confident way the line is usually quoted.

items.why: The words come to us through someone else’s recollection at a hearing, not through anything Rockefeller wrote or was recorded saying. Wikiquote ↗ files the entry as Disputed for that reason.

Wikiquote records that Rockefeller doubted he had said this, citing David Freeman Hawke’s John D.: The Founding Father of the Rockefellers (1980). A denial is not decisive on its own, but it is the opposite of corroboration the entry ↗.

“But he said unto them, I have meat to eat that ye know not of” King James Version ↗. Wikiquote raises the parallel itself. Remembered speech tends to drift toward familiar cadences, and few cadences were more familiar than this one.

We searched six digitized volumes of the 1879 New York railroad inquiry and found no Isaac Hewitt and no such sentence the proceedings ↗. OCR is imperfect and we did not search exhaustively, so this settles nothing — but we could not verify the citation, and we would rather say so than repeat it as though we had.

misattribution.truthLine: Treat this as something a witness said Rockefeller said, in 1879, and that Rockefeller denied — not as a documented Rockefeller quotation Wikiquote, Disputed ↗.

context.heading: Why a hostile quotation sticks
lead: Rockefeller spent decades in front of committees and grand juries, and a great deal of the folklore about him was generated there rather than by him. Testimony is sworn, published and quotable, which gives a remembered remark the surface texture of a document even when it is only a memory.

This particular sentence also does something useful for the person retelling it: it makes Rockefeller sound knowing and slightly sinister, which is exactly the character the era’s critics were trying to draw. Lines that confirm what an audience already suspects are the ones that survive.
context.pull: It reaches us as something a witness said he said — which is not the same thing as a quotation.
